title: Money, reviewed
hookLine: earn, share, remember: the three pillars in the budget
tomorrow: the aunties are whispering about Aman. what do the Gurus ask for?

lines: MIDNIGHT, AND A LOT OF RED.
cards: Midnight, two days before the wedding, and the budget spreadsheet is open on Jasleen's laptop with a lot of red in it. Aman's paycheck is gone.
Aman's mother still wants the bigger hall for the reception, and the DJ, and the second photographer. Jasleen wants to cancel all of it. Aman says nothing at all, which is worse.
Simran, who only came over to help with the seating chart, is now sitting between two people trying very hard not to fight. Then Bebe, who never touches laptops, asks for a pen.

teach.b: On the back of an envelope, Bebe writes three words in Gurmukhi and draws three columns.

teach.h: NAAM, KIRAT, VAND: THE THREE PILLARS.
teach.b: Sikhs often sum up Guru Nanak's way in three pillars: naam japna, remembering God; kirat karni, earning by honest work; vand chhakna, sharing what you have.
Two of them sit in one line on ang 1245, where Guru Nanak says, in paraphrase, the one who earns by honest work and gives some of it away recognizes the path.

teach.h: EARN, SHARE, REMEMBER, AS A BUDGET.
teach.b: Over this week those pillars have been hiding in plain sight: a share for others, giving wisely, a gift and not a ranking, rising anyway, serving after the paycheck stops. Bebe turns them into a budget.
Earn: what do we honestly have, today, without borrowing to impress anyone? Share: what in this wedding feeds people? Some Sikh families serve the wedding meal as langar, everyone fed the same food.
Remember: what is this day actually for? The Anand Karaj, the wedding itself, is the couple walking around the Guru Granth Sahib while the lavan are sung.

teach.h: THE WEDDING ITSELF COSTS ALMOST NOTHING.

teach.b: Aman's mother looks at the three columns for a long time. Then she crosses out the second photographer herself.

how: Sikhs often summarize Guru Nanak's teaching as naam japna, kirat karni and vand chhakna, and some families apply them to money through honest earning, daswandh and langar.

o: something to earn honestly, share, and spend remembering God
something a devout Sikh should avoid thinking about
a reward God gives the people who pray most

p: the wedding: lavan around the Granth

s: a Sikh wedding has to be expensive to count
the Anand Karaj is the couple walking around the Guru Granth Sahib while the lavan are sung; that part costs almost nothing.
ang 1245 pairs honest earning with giving some of it away
two of the three pillars in one line of Guru Nanak's.
the three pillars are about prayer, so money isn't part of them
kirat and vand are about money: earning it honestly, sharing it freely.

games.q: your sibling wants a loan to throw a party big enough to impress the relatives. going by Bebe's three columns, what's the first question?
o: what do we honestly have, without borrowing to impress anyone?
how many relatives need impressing, and which ones matter most?
can the loan be paid off before anyone finds out about it?
games.why: Bebe's first column is earn: what you honestly have, today. then share, then remember what the day is for.

practice: Count on your fingers three recent things your money did. One you earned honestly and are glad of. One that fed or helped someone else.
One that helped you remember what matters. If a column comes up empty, just notice it, without judging, and rest there for the sit.

wordCard.voice: Money. In Sikhi, something to earn honestly, share freely, and spend with God remembered.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: vand chhakna, sharing what you have, one of the three pillars.

carryVoice: Your line: earn, share, remember, three columns on the back of one envelope. Two days to the wedding.

sources.ref: Ang 1245 (Sarang ki Var, salok of Guru Nanak: ghaal khaae kichh hathhu dehi), paraphrased
Sikh tradition: naam japna, kirat karni, vand chhakna as a summary of Guru Nanak's teaching
